title: Introducing Pipeline Revival: give old opportunities a new reason to talk
summary: Connect fresh signals to past buying conversations, prioritize revival opportunities, and prepare contextual outreach for reps to review in Slack.
body_markdown:
The Pipeline Revival Agent is a concrete example of what you can build on Cedar: a workflow that finds a reason to reopen an old opportunity, decides which prospects deserve attention, and prepares a message grounded in the conversation you already had.


It brings together the layers introduced in[Cedar Blocks](https://mail.cedarcopilot.com/blog/cedar-blocks) . The data layer preserves the buying context. Sales intelligence helps decide where to focus. The agent turns that context into a draft, then brings it to the rep in Slack for review.


The launch film walks through that sequence. Here is a closer look at each step and why it matters.


## Start with the people who already showed interest


Your CRM contains people who were interested enough to book a demo, explain their problem, and spend time evaluating your product. Some of those conversations stopped because the timing was wrong. Others stalled around a missing capability or an existing vendor agreement.


A closed-lost record can hold useful buying context long after the opportunity leaves the active pipeline. The prospect may have described a specific workflow they wanted to improve, a condition they needed you to meet, or a date when they expected to revisit the decision. Those details give a future conversation somewhere useful to begin.


In the launch, Isabelle describes a habit of strong reps ramping into a new role: they go through old CRM records and look for prospects they can revive. That requires reading the history, understanding why each conversation stopped, and deciding whether there is a credible reason to reach out again.


The Pipeline Revival Agent builds around that same work. It combines the original conversation with relevant changes so the rep can spend more time assessing a good opening and less time reconstructing an old deal.


## Find a reason to reconnect now


The first step is timing. An old opportunity becomes more interesting when something changes that relates to the buyer's original situation. The launch highlights three kinds of signals.


### A prospect says something relevant


A LinkedIn post can reveal a current priority or a problem the person is thinking about. Its value comes from the connection to the earlier buying conversation. A post about expanding a team, for example, could be relevant to a prospect who previously described a workflow that would become difficult at a larger scale.


That is an illustrative reason to investigate, rather than proof that the person wants to buy. The agent's job is to bring the change and the original context together so a rep can judge the opportunity.


### A competitor's renewal approaches


A buyer may have mentioned when their current vendor agreement renews. That date gives the team a more useful time to revisit the conversation than an arbitrary follow-up interval.


The original discussion still matters. A renewal creates an opening to ask whether the buyer's priorities have changed; the reasons they considered your product help make that question specific.


### Your product changes


A product launch can address something that previously blocked a deal. The team needs to connect the new capability to the people who asked for it, understand how important it was to their decision, and explain what has changed.


This makes revival a useful extension of a launch. Alongside announcing the feature broadly, the team can prepare focused follow-ups for prospects whose earlier conversations make the release especially relevant.


## Use the data layer to find the right prospects


Working backward from a new feature to old opportunities is difficult when the relevant details live across meeting transcripts and CRM records. A rep or agent has to find the conversations, read them, and work out whether a passing mention represented a real buying requirement.


Cedar's[data layer](https://mail.cedarcopilot.com/platform/data) gives the revival workflow structured context to work with. The launch shows an agent filtering closed-lost deals by extracted pain points and requested features related to a new release. The agent can start with that relevant set instead of rereading the entire meeting history for every campaign.


The useful output is a list with a reason behind each match. A feature name alone gives the rep very little to work with. The underlying context explains what the prospect wanted to accomplish and why that capability mattered.


For example, imagine a prospect previously needed an integration to keep a particular handoff from becoming manual. When that integration becomes available, the revival opportunity is the workflow it enables. Connecting the release to the earlier problem gives the rep a concrete explanation to evaluate and use.


The quality of this step depends on the available history and the signals the team has configured Cedar to extract. The goal is to make relevant buying context reusable across the workflow.


## Prioritize with a revival fit score


A list of relevant prospects still leaves a practical question: which conversations should the rep work on first?


The launch uses Cedar's sales intelligence layer to assign a revival fit score. It combines three considerations: the annual contract value, how strong the original opportunity was, and how compelling the reason to reconnect is now.


Those considerations answer different questions. Contract value describes the potential size of the opportunity. Original deal quality reflects whether there was a meaningful fit and buying conversation. The current revival reason captures what makes this moment worth revisiting.


Looking at them together helps avoid treating every match as equally urgent. A large potential deal with a weak connection to the new signal may deserve less immediate attention than a strong prior opportunity whose main blocker has just changed.


The score gives the rep a way to organize attention. The supporting reasons provide the context needed to decide whether that ordering makes sense. That is especially useful when a rep has a short block of time and needs a manageable set of conversations to work through.


## Draft from the original buying context


Once the agent has identified and prioritized a prospect, it can prepare the message. The launch describes a draft that draws on the original conversation and can bring in product launches, case studies, or other relevant materials.


A useful revival message explains the connection clearly: here is the problem you raised, here is what changed, and here is why it might be worth another look. The detail comes from the buying history, giving the rep something more substantial to review than a name inserted into a template.


Supporting material should help make that connection. A release announcement can show the new capability. A relevant case study can help the prospect understand how a similar workflow could work. The agent can gather those materials while preparing the draft, so the rep has both the message and its supporting context together.


Continuing the illustrative integration example, the opening would refer to the handoff the prospect wanted to improve and explain that the newly available integration addresses that specific issue. A short invitation to revisit the workflow follows naturally from that change.


## Bring the draft to the rep in Slack


The final step in the film is a Slack notification with the completed draft and the context the rep needs to refine it.


That handoff connects the background research to the rep's working day. The rep can assess why the opportunity resurfaced, read the proposed message, and adjust the language or next step to fit the relationship. The[Pipeline Revival workflow](https://mail.cedarcopilot.com/agent-library/pipeline-revival) retains that review point before outreach.


Isabelle closes with the idea of using a spare 30-minute block to work through revival opportunities. The preparation happens earlier in the workflow: relevant changes are connected to buying history, prospects are prioritized, and drafts are ready for attention.


That is the practical advantage of building the agent on shared infrastructure. The same deal context supports discovery, prioritization, and writing, while the rep receives a coherent piece of work they can act on. An old conversation becomes easier to revisit when the reason, evidence, and next message arrive together.
